questions.question: What is WebRTC?

options.text: A web framework
A technology enabling real-time peer-to-peer communication (audio, video, data) in browsers
A database
A server technology

questions.explanation: WebRTC (Web Real-Time Communication): browser API for peer-to-peer audio, video, and data. No plugins needed. Powers: video calls, screen sharing, file transfer, gaming. Direct browser-to-browser communication.

questions.question: What makes WebRTC different from WebSockets?

options.text: They are the same
WebRTC is peer-to-peer and optimized for media; WebSockets go through a server
WebSockets are faster
WebRTC requires plugins

questions.explanation: WebRTC: peer-to-peer (direct between browsers), optimized for real-time media (adaptive bitrate, jitter buffers). WebSockets: client-server, general-purpose bidirectional. Different use cases.

questions.question: What is a signaling server in WebRTC?

options.text: A server that routes all media traffic between peers
A server that helps peers discover each other and exchange connection information
A media transcoding server for format conversion
A database server for storing session state

questions.explanation: Signaling server: coordinates connection setup. Exchanges: SDP (session description), ICE candidates (network paths). Not part of WebRTC spec—use WebSockets, HTTP, etc. Once connected, peers communicate directly.

questions.question: What is ICE in WebRTC?

options.text: Internet Connection Establishment—a protocol for secure connections
Interactive Connectivity Establishment—a framework for finding the best path between peers
A video codec for real-time communication
An encryption method for media streams

questions.explanation: ICE: finds network path between peers. Gathers candidates: local IP, server-reflexive (STUN), relay (TURN). Tests connectivity. Handles NAT traversal. Essential for peer-to-peer in real networks.

questions.question: What is STUN in WebRTC?

options.text: Secure Transport Unified Network—a protocol for encrypted communication
Session Traversal Utilities for NAT—helps discover public IP and port for NAT traversal
A video format for streaming media
A distributed database for session storage

questions.explanation: STUN server: tells client its public IP/port (as seen from outside NAT). Client uses this for ICE candidates. Lightweight, stateless. Works when NAT allows direct connection. Free STUN servers available.

questions.question: What is TURN in WebRTC?

options.text: Transport Unified Relay Network—a protocol for load balancing
Traversal Using Relays around NAT—relays traffic when direct connection isn't possible
A video codec for high-quality streaming
A signaling protocol for session establishment

questions.explanation: TURN server: relays media when direct connection fails (symmetric NAT, firewalls). All traffic goes through TURN. More expensive (bandwidth), but ensures connectivity. Fallback when STUN fails.

questions.question: What is SDP in WebRTC?

options.text: Secure Data Protocol—an encryption standard for media
Session Description Protocol—describes media capabilities, codecs, and connection information
A video format for peer-to-peer streaming
A database query language for session data

questions.explanation: SDP: text format describing session. Contains: media types, codecs, encryption keys, ICE candidates. Exchanged via signaling. Offer/answer model: caller sends offer, callee sends answer. Negotiates capabilities.

questions.question: What are common use cases for WebRTC?

options.text: Video conferencing (Zoom, Google Meet)
Screen sharing and remote desktop
Peer-to-peer file sharing
All of the above

questions.explanation: WebRTC use cases: video calls (Zoom, Meet, Teams), screen sharing, P2P file transfer, online gaming, IoT communication, live streaming (low latency). Any real-time browser communication.

questions.question: Is WebRTC encrypted?

options.text: No, it's plain text
Yes—DTLS for data channels, SRTP for media; encryption is mandatory
Only optionally
Only for video

questions.explanation: WebRTC security: encryption mandatory. DTLS (Datagram TLS) for data channels. SRTP (Secure RTP) for media. Keys exchanged via DTLS-SRTP. End-to-end encrypted by default. Can't disable.

questions.question: What is a data channel in WebRTC?

options.text: A dedicated network path for video streaming
A peer-to-peer channel for sending arbitrary data (text, files, game state)
A database connection for real-time queries
A video stream with embedded metadata

questions.explanation: Data channel: P2P data transfer. Like WebSocket but peer-to-peer. Configurable: reliable/unreliable, ordered/unordered. Use cases: chat, file transfer, game state sync. Low latency, no server relay.

questions.question: What is the challenge of scaling WebRTC for large video conferences?

options.text: No challenges
Peer-to-peer doesn't scale—need SFU or MCU servers to relay/mix streams
WebRTC is always scalable
Just add more browsers

questions.explanation: Scaling challenge: P2P mesh doesn't scale (n² connections). Solutions: SFU (Selective Forwarding Unit)—server relays streams, each client sends once. MCU (Multipoint Control Unit)—server mixes into one stream. Most use SFU.

questions.question: A company wants to build a video calling feature in their web app. What technology enables this without plugins?

options.text: Flash
WebRTC—native browser support for real-time video/audio
Java Applets
Silverlight

questions.explanation: WebRTC: native in all modern browsers (Chrome, Firefox, Safari, Edge). No plugins. getUserMedia for camera/mic access, RTCPeerConnection for P2P. Standard approach for browser-based video calling.
